studios.name: Barely Dressed Pictures
studios.details: An independent legacy label built around mysteries and the Sebastian Rook character. Recent films mix returning collaborators with short commissions for younger directors.

studios.name: Second Take Features

studios.name: Electric Marquee

studios.name: Fourth Wall Pictures
studios.details: A theatre-adaptation company whose rehearsal methods connect filmmakers from several generations. Long gaps between projects reflect stage commitments and financing.

studios.name: Available Light Cooperative
studios.details: A cooperative of directors, editors and sound recordists. Members share resources while making distinct productions and maintaining their own documentary work.

standalone_texts.title: A Return, Not a Reprise
standalone_texts.details: An oral-history transcript about Cressida’s guest appearance and the difference between repeating an old performance and returning to work.
standalone_texts.content:
**Excerpt from a conversation during a break on the final day. June's questions and Cressida's replies were lightly edited for length.**

**June:** Did you want to see the old films before coming back?

**Cressida:** No. You can end up trying to impersonate yourself. I wanted to know where the chair was, who had been in the room before me and why nobody wanted to mention the missing take. Those are useful questions. Whether I could still raise an eyebrow exactly as I did in nineteen sixty-four was not a useful question.

**June:** You asked to rehearse the entrance without the camera.

**Cressida:** I asked to walk it. Rehearsal sounds grand. At my age, knowing where the floor changes matters. Then I could stop thinking about the floor and listen to the person in front of me.

**June:** Was the set very different?

**Cressida:** Quieter in some ways. There were more people watching little screens, but the person beside the camera was still waiting for something truthful to happen. I recognised that. I also recognised the rush to get a scene finished before the light went. Nobody has invented a longer afternoon.

**June:** Did the guest part feel like a farewell?

**Cressida:** A working day. A good one. If somebody wants a farewell, they can write one in the programme. I had a scene to do.

*Archive note: this conversation concerns the 2025 guest appearance. The photographs from the 1960s remain a separate publicity series.*

standalone_texts.content:
## Before the camera arrives

Walk the route in ordinary shoes first. Mark the change from dry ground to wet ground. Move the bags that will not be in the finished frame; do not learn a route around temporary clutter and then forget why the route changed.

The rehearsal is also an acting rehearsal. The escort knows where she is going. Lucia must know where the camera is going. Those are different pieces of information, and the second should not be visible in the first.

## The pause at the door

The handler has the stillest part of the scene. Give him the space to remain still. An extra adjustment from the escort can make his hesitation look like a reaction to movement instead of a choice he has already made.

Try the line before the turn, then after it. Keep the version in which the breath belongs to the thought. Do not choose the version only because it makes the action look harder.

## After the rain

The photograph everybody likes was taken after the interesting work had finished. We were dealing with wet coats and the last equipment cases. That is part of a location day too.

I perform all my own stunts. I have never used a stunt double. That does not make the preparation a solo job: the coordinator, camera crew and other performers all know things I need to know. The point is to arrive at the take with enough shared preparation that I can play the scene.

*Personal notebook selection, assembled the morning after the location wrap. This is a record of creative decisions, not a stunt instruction sheet.*

standalone_texts.title: Darius King: The Coat-Check Pages
standalone_texts.details: An annotated interview excerpt about building the auction-caper character around what he does with a borrowed coat.
standalone_texts.content:
**Interview fragment, retained with the auction-caper publicity material.**

The coat was useful because it let Darius give the character a small private task. He did not want to keep checking the stolen object. He wanted to keep checking whether the coat still looked as though it belonged to him.

“In the first rehearsal I straightened the lapel every time someone spoke. It was too much. You could see the actor demonstrating a nervous man. We kept one adjustment and let the rest of the worry move into the listening.”

The upward camera angle made an ordinary step look more decisive. Darius and the camera operator tried the movement at several speeds before choosing the unhurried version. The joke needed the character to believe that he was proceeding sensibly.

Amina's dialogue was quicker than his first reading. The scene improved when he stopped trying to put a joke on every line. The coat-check attendant could do the noticing; his character only needed to remain magnificently unaware of it.

### Margin added after the screening

The audience laughed before the explanation. Leave that space in future performances. The silence is doing a job, even when it feels long from inside the scene.

*The surviving page ends here. A later publicity summary describes the same exchange more neatly, but this version keeps the hesitation.*

standalone_texts.title: Listening Before the Chase
standalone_texts.details: Nia and Dev compare the actor’s listening cues with the sound edit in a convention-floor stakeout.
standalone_texts.content:
### Nia's note

The stakeout only works if listening looks active. I tried watching each person who passed the table, but that made the character seem certain of what she was looking for. The better version was to stay with the conversation while letting one unfamiliar sound pull my attention away.

### Dev's reply

We had three possible cues in the early sound edit: the lift, the public-address system and the noise from the exhibition stand. Using all three explained the room too completely. We kept the public-address interruption and let the other sounds remain part of the general crowd.

### What changed in the next pass

Nia's reaction no longer landed exactly on the loudest sound. It came slightly before the audience could confidently identify it. That made the character seem observant without turning the moment into a demonstration.

The chase begins later. This page belongs to the waiting scene. Keeping the two rhythms separate gave the movement somewhere to grow.

There is no claim here that the sound cue was present during every take. The location recording and the finished scene are different records of the same work. The interview preserves that distinction because it explains why a convincing reaction can be built from several small decisions rather than one perfectly timed accident.

standalone_texts.title: One Screening, Two Cuts
standalone_texts.details: An exchange between an editor and a performer after a small screening, preserving their disagreement over a reaction shot.
standalone_texts.content:
**Noor to Amara, after the small screening**

I think we should keep the longer reaction. In the short version you seem to understand the missing take immediately. In the room, people were still deciding whether to trust the story. Your extra moment gives them permission to wait.

**Amara's reply**

I like the uncertainty, but I do not think it comes from holding my face. Listen to the breath before the answer. That is where I am deciding what to tell them. If we stay after the answer, it begins to look as though I am inviting the audience to judge it.

**Noor**

I tried your version without the room sound dropping away. You were right about the breath. I still miss the glance toward the empty chair.

**Amara**

Could the glance belong earlier, while somebody else is talking? Then it is something the character does, rather than an illustration of the line.

### Screening note

Both cuts were retained in the working folder. The next screening used the earlier glance and the shorter hold after the answer. Nobody recorded a final vote. The useful part of the exchange was the distinction between uncertainty in the performance and uncertainty added by the edit.

*Correspondence retained with the screening notes; both working cuts remained in the edit folder.*

standalone_texts.title: Elias Grant: Notes in the Radio Margin
standalone_texts.details: A young actor’s marked-up radio rehearsal pages, kept separately from the later Rook publicity.
standalone_texts.content:
## Page with the first entrance

**Crossed out:** sound older.

**Written underneath:** know why you are calling.

The first recording has too much weight on the opening words. I was trying to make the listener understand the whole character before the scene had begun. The later pass is lighter. It leaves room for the character to be wrong.

## A useful direction

Do not answer the pause. Answer the person.

The delay in the remote session made every gap feel meaningful, even when someone was only waiting for the connection. We ran the exchange once without trying to repair those gaps. Some of the awkwardness belonged to the scene after all.

## Kept for the next job

Mark the thought, not only the breath. If I mark every breath I start obeying the pencil. If I know what changes halfway through the sentence, the breath usually finds its own place.

*These pages were kept after the December 2022 radio rehearsal. Elias had recently turned eighteen. They precede the later screen publicity and do not describe a Rook performance.*

standalone_texts.title: Kenji Watanari: A Location Ledger
standalone_texts.details: A photographer’s retrospective location ledger recording what changed between a first visit and a later return.
standalone_texts.content:
- **First survey:** A long concrete passage, a red maintenance light and traffic heard above the frame.
- **Camera rehearsal:** The apparent exit falls outside the selected view. The actor can leave without the image explaining where he has gone.
- **Return visit:** New paint has made the wall brighter. The sound of the road is still more useful than the signs.

A photograph can make an empty place look as though it is waiting for a person. The location film needed the opposite: a person who briefly enters a place that already has its own business.

Kenji's first contact prints gave the figure too much weight. He moved the camera back and kept the awkward strip of wall at the edge. That strip is not a clue. It is the part of the place that refuses to become a clue.

Ten years later, the notebook is less useful as a map than as a record of attention. Several details that seemed essential on the survey never reached the finished frame. One sound, written down almost as an afterthought, remained in the discussion of the scene.

*Retrospective ledger assembled from location notes and later observations. Dates refer to the archive entry; the associated film retains its original production date.*
